records.our_prose: Pick English cucumbers while they are firm and glossy. The long ones are usually picked at about 12 to 14 inches and the short Beit Alpha types at about 5 to 8 inches. Cut or clip the stem instead of pulling, because the skin and vine are tender. They grow fast, ready in a couple of weeks once they set, so check every day or two. The thin skin does not need peeling, and picking often keeps more cucumbers coming.

records.our_prose: Harvest English cucumbers young and often, while the skin is glossy and firm. Pick the long Dutch or English types at about 12 to 14 inches (the USDA fresh-market minimum is 11 inches) and the shorter Beit Alpha and mini types at about 5 to 8 inches, cutting or clipping the stem rather than pulling, since the thin-skinned fruit and brittle vine bruise easily. Fruit sizes up fast, often reaching pickable size within about 10 to 11 days of set, so check every 1 to 2 days at peak. The thin, tender skin needs no peeling. Pick promptly, because an overheld fruit stops the plant setting new ones and the crop keeps best when cut young.

records.source_context: Spider Mites Two-spotted spider mites ( Tetranychus urticae ) can be a serious problem on cucurbits, especially on watermelons and cantaloupes, during hot, dry weather. This damage appears as pale yellow and reddish-brown spots ranging in size from small specks to large whitish, stippled areas on the upper sides of leaves.

records.our_prose: In California's interior valleys (zones 8 to 9) cucumber has a long, warm growing season. Direct-sow from spring once frost has passed and the soil warms, with successions every few weeks into early summer for a continuous supply. The long, hot summer extends the window, but keep moisture steady and mulched through the heat to prevent bitterness.

records.our_prose: Along California's cooler north and north coast (zones 9 to 10), cucumber is a warm-season crop that wants the warmest, sunniest spot. Plant in spring once frost has passed, then plant again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the peak of summer, when heat and pests make cucumbers struggle and turn bitter.

records.our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs English cucumbers on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 60 days later, around May 14, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, vines stop setting fruit and any that does form turns bitter. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for English cucumbers, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

records.our_prose: In the warm arid Southwest (southern New Mexico and West Texas, zone 8), cucumber is a warm-season crop with a long window. Sow after the last frost once the soil warms, with successions into early summer; the intense heat and low humidity make steady, deep watering and mulch essential to prevent bitterness and spider mites. A fall sowing extends harvest into the mild autumn.

records.our_prose: Try not to grow cucumbers or their relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so, and clean up old vines at the end of the season. Under cover, use fresh growing medium between crops if disease has been a problem. Also keep English cucumbers away from ordinary cucumbers so bees cannot cross-pollinate them.

records.our_prose: Aim for even, steady moisture, roughly 1 inch of water per week and more in heat or in fast-draining substrate, delivered deeply rather than in light daily sprinkles. English cucumbers are bred to be mild and are far less prone to the classic stress-bitterness of open-field slicers, but steady water still drives straight, well-filled fruit and keeps the plant cropping.
